lines: A hundred hours. One patch of sky. And absolutely nothing there.
At least, that's what it looked like, until the James Webb Space Telescope kept staring.
What came back was more than two thousand five hundred sources, hiding in the dark.
This is Webb's deepest look yet.
Look up at the Moon. Now imagine a patch of sky just one tenth as wide.
That tiny square sits in the constellation Fornax, and from the ground, it looks almost completely empty.
Astronomers call a view like this a deep field. The idea is simple, and a little crazy: point a telescope at the emptiest place you can find, and never look away.
In 2003, Hubble did exactly that. And the darkness turned out to be anything but empty.
Between September 2003 and January 2004, the Hubble Space Telescope stared at this patch.
It took eight hundred exposures, across four hundred orbits of Earth, adding up to eleven point three days of light.
The result was the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, with nearly ten thousand galaxies, in a patch a tenth the width of the Moon.
But Hubble mostly sees visible light. And the earliest galaxies, and the dustiest ones, hide from it.
To find them, we needed a different kind of eye.
Here's the problem. The universe is expanding, so light from the most distant galaxies gets stretched on its long journey.
Blue light becomes red. Red light slides out of our sight entirely, into the infrared. Astronomers call this redshift.
Dust does something similar. It soaks up starlight, and glows quietly in the infrared.
So to see the early universe, you have to see heat.
Enter Webb. A six and a half metre mirror, made of eighteen gold-coated hexagons.
Behind it, a five-layer sunshield, as big as a tennis court, keeps the whole telescope freezing cold.
Because infrared light is heat. And a warm telescope would be blinded by its own glow.
But one instrument on Webb needs to be even colder. It's called MIRI, the Mid-Infrared Instrument, and it sees wavelengths from five to twenty-eight microns.
The sunshield alone cools it to about ninety kelvin. That's still far too warm.
So Webb carries a dedicated cryocooler, a helium refrigerator, that drags MIRI's detectors down to under seven kelvin.
Every single degree warmer makes the detector's own noise about ten times worse.
In April 2022, MIRI reached six point four kelvin. Just a few degrees above absolute zero.
Now it was ready to stare.
The target was Hubble's classic field, in a survey called MIDIS, the MIRI Deep Imaging Survey.
Nearly a hundred hours of observing, across MIRI's shortest-wavelength filters, combined with Webb's near-infrared camera.
Forty-one of those hours went into a single filter, the longest Webb has ever spent on an extragalactic field in one filter.
Watch what happens as the hours pile up. At first, there's only noise.
Photon by photon, the faintest light builds up. Smudges become shapes. Shapes become galaxies.
Each extra hour reveals fainter, older, more distant things.
To be fair, it is not Webb's longest stare overall. In 2025 it spent more than a hundred and twenty hours on the galaxy cluster Abell S1063.
When the image was finished, astronomers counted more than two thousand five hundred sources in this tiny patch.
Orange and red ones are dusty galaxies, or old stars from the early universe.
Small, greenish-white ones are especially distant, their light stretched far into the infrared.
And the blue and cyan galaxies shine brightest in the near-infrared.
More than five hundred galaxies already have measured distances, some as far as redshift eleven.
Around twenty-five look like they're from the first billion years.
And more than a hundred are so red, they're nearly invisible without Webb.
One of them is a little red dot nicknamed Virgil, at a redshift of about six point six.
In near-infrared alone, it looked faint and ordinary. But MIRI revealed an extremely red glow, and the first clear detection of the galaxy hosting one of these little red dots.
That glow hints at an active black hole inside. Something Webb's other cameras completely missed.
Look deeper, and you reach cosmic dawn, when the first stars lit up.
In 2024, the JADES survey confirmed a galaxy at redshift fourteen point three two, seen just two hundred ninety million years after the Big Bang.
And in January 2026, a galaxy called MoM-z14 pushed that to redshift fourteen point four four, about two hundred eighty million years after the Big Bang.
And Webb isn't done.
A hundred hours of staring at nothing, and the nothing was full.
What should Webb look at next? Tell us below, and subscribe to Technical Talk India.
Webb stared at one empty patch of sky for a hundred hours.
Here's what it found.
That patch is only a tenth as wide as the full Moon.
Hour by hour, the darkness fills with light.
Galaxies that Hubble never saw start to appear.
Some are so distant, their light is stretched into the infrared.
Dusty, red, and ancient.
More than two thousand five hundred sources, in a speck of sky.
Hundreds are extremely red.
Some date to just two hundred eighty million years after the Big Bang.
